Subject: Pricing and batching questions — Redwood

Thanks for the demo today, Aditya — that was helpful. A couple follow-ups from our side focused on cost and performance as we model the integration: 

- Can you confirm target unit economics (what Redwood charges per 1M tokens) for a production workload?
- We have continuous inference across user sessions (always-on background scoring). What batching assumptions should we use when estimating latency and cost?
- Typical request size: 150 tokens prompt + 50 tokens completion on average, across 20M inference calls/month. How should we think about concurrency and batching to estimate $/1M tokens?

Also curious about burst behavior — we see traffic spikes up to 10x for short windows. What do you assume for concurrency and burst capacity?

Thanks — can you send a short post-call recap with the assumptions you use so our finance team can model it?

— Alex

Subject: Re: Pricing and batching questions — Redwood

Hi Alex — great talking yesterday. Quick post-call recap and the assumptions we typically use for cost modelling. Below is a concise set you can hand to finance/infra folks. Happy to walk through numbers live.

Summary (high level):
- Target list price (hosted API): $X per 1M prompt+completion tokens (we'll put exact bracket in the attached pricing model). Discounts and Dedicated pricing vary by committed volume.
- Unit economics depend materially on batching & concurrency. Continuous batching reduces per-token compute by amortizing kernel startup and overlapping attention work.

Assumptions to model: 
1) Token accounting: prompt + completion counted together. Use your stated 200 tokens/request average.
2) Continuous batching profile: for always-on scoring workloads we assume a base steady-state QPS that yields effective batch sizes in 8–32 tokens per forward (this maps to 8–32 requests aggregated per micro-batch depending on prompt length and model).
3) Concurrency and latency SLOs: for a 100 ms target tail latency we provision for higher concurrency and lower batching; for 500 ms SLO we can increase batching which lowers unit cost. Typical SLO tradeoffs: 100–200 ms (low batching) vs 300–800 ms (higher batching).
4) Burst multiplier: assume short bursts up to 5–10x. We recommend autoscaling + a burst lane (Dedicated or higher tier Hosted) to avoid throttling; bursts increase cost but only for the burst window.
5) Monthly volume: your example of 20M calls @200 tokens => 4B tokens/month. At a sample list price of $Y/1M tokens (see attachment), that maps to $Z/month before discounts and caching optimizations.

Attachments: redwood-pricing-model.xlsx (pricing brackets, illustrative math for your volumes and different SLOs).

Next steps I propose:
- Marissa (SE) & Lauren (Solutions) to confirm batching/concurrency impact on the model we attached.
- We’ll provide a short POC proposal and recommended Dedicated sizing if you want a committed-capacity quote.

If you can share a little more on peak QPS and desired latency target, we’ll return a tighter $/1M token estimate.

Best,
Aditya Rao
Account Executive | Redwood Inference
From: Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.com>

Looping in a few technical notes for the pricing model: 

- Continuous batching: our runtime uses a rolling batching window (10–50 ms) for low-latency scoring workloads. For small prompts (<=200 tokens) that matches the 8–32 request batch sizes Aditya called out. For larger prompts the effective batch size measured in tokens increases but request-level batching may be smaller.
- Concurrency impact: per-token GPU utilization increases with batch size — unit cost declines roughly linearly up to the saturation point for that model/hardware combo (model dependent). We use conservative 20–30% cost reduction at median batch sizes for scheduling.
- KV cache behavior: cached prefixes dramatically reduce compute for multi-turn chat vs stateless scoring — make sure finance models stateless vs cached flows separately.
- Burst handling: autoscale + burst lanes are recommended. For Dedicated we size a headroom buffer (~20–30%) for predictable headroom; hosted customers can use on-demand burst which is priced at a premium for short windows.

I’ll validate the numbers in the attached spreadsheet and add a small worked example (20M calls @200 tokens -> cost table for latency SLOs and Dedicated sizing).

— Marissa
Marissa Cole
Senior Sales Engineer | Redwood Inference

Subject: Re: Pricing and batching questions — Redwood

Appreciate the budget context, Sam — that helps. Quick answers and next steps below.

Short answers (ballpark, per 1M prompt+completion tokens):
- 100–200 ms SLO (low batching): ~$120–$160 / 1M tokens (hosted list price; effective unit cost falls with committed Dedicated capacity).
- 300–800 ms SLO (higher batching): ~$60–$90 / 1M tokens.
- Hosted burst lane premium: model ~1.5x–2x the effective per-token rate during the burst window; Dedicated headroom is typically modeled as 20–30% extra capacity in the committed sizing (no per-burst premium but increases committed cost).

Mapping to your 4B tokens/month example: 
- At $120/1M => ~$480k/month (hosted, low-latency) — outside your stated budget.
- At $75/1M => ~$300k/month (higher batching / relaxed SLO) — still above $100k/mo.

What this implies: to hit $40k–$100k/month with 4B tokens you need either: 
- lower effective token count via caching and shorter completions, or
- a lower commitments/volume profile (fewer tokens), or
- a very aggressive Dedicated discount (we can run numbers if you provide target committed spend).

Next steps I propose: 
1) We’ll share an updated pricing model (attached) with explicit per-SLO rows and a worked example mapping to your budget brackets.
2) If you want a tighter Dedicated quote, please share a 12-month commit target (monthly tokens or $/month).
3) Quick follow-up call this week to walk through options — available Thu/Fri.

I’ll also have Marissa add the worked numeric examples into the spreadsheet and send back.

Best,
Aditya Rao
Account Executive | Redwood Inference
